I'm not from India, but I thought that I'll share my own thoughts on this matter. First, it's not just Indian languages that gets an increasing amount of 'English' loan-words into their languages. It is literally the entire part of the world where science and innovation are seen as important! 
(There has 'crept' in a steadily increasing amount of 'English' loan-words into my language as well - Swedish, Scandinavia in Northern Europe. And the situation is pretty  much the same in all the different languages in the EU [Europe], at the very least. Probably many, many more still though- if I'm allowed to guess. We have to remember though that these words in question are usually 'made up', constructed, or simply named after or by an inventor - since the absolute majority of these words are meant to describe things, circumstances, etc., that simply didn't even exist, or was "a thing" before. [Although not exactly always, admittedly.]. Most languages ['pure English] included] would really struggle to make up a new word for something that has never existed before - often not even something remotely similar, without it sounding either archaic, cumbersome or even out-right laughable.
And the reason I have written 'English' all this time? Well, it's simply because English is probably one of the most 'mixed' languages that exists (no, honestly!). Around the year 0 it was ruled and influenced by the Romans, and their Latin - that rapidly [or at least within a couple of hundred years after the spread and adoption of Christianity, it became THE undisputed language of writing, scholarship and learning in general....alongside with a bit of Greek, for 'obvious' reasons.] Sure, the Romans did adopt some Greek into their language - but the 'real reason' for Latin's newfound 'status' was both because that the liturgics, that is both the written as well as oral sermons and 'services' was delivered in Latin. And the Greek language - from which all the Church-doctrines + related texts were interpreted - also had a 'special place' in some of these places and people.
